summary: Earth Jukebox turns NASA Earth visualizations into sound, so people who cannot see a color map can still explore the data. Two tracks sweep across a NASA visualization with a moving playhead: the temperature of the world’s oceans, and global air pollution. It comes with an accessible web page, tested with a screen reader, and an optional Arduino device that shows the same data by touch and light.
details:
The problem. NASA’s Earth Information Center publishes striking visualizations of our changing planet, but they are made to be seen. Blind and low-vision people, and anyone who cannot read a colour-coded map, are shut out of the science. [Add one sentence on why this matters to you.]

The vision. If you can hear where the ocean is warm, or where the air is heavy with pollution, a map becomes something you can listen to and explore. I wanted the sound to be musical enough to enjoy and honest enough to trust.

How it works. For each track, one frame of a NASA video is turned into a grid of values: 64 steps from west to east, by five bands of latitude. Each cell becomes a note. Pitch and loudness follow the data, notes are snapped to a five-note scale so it stays musical, and empty cells are silent. A white playhead line moves across the picture in step with the sound.

  • Sea surface temperature: the map’s own colour legend (0 to 32 °C) is used to turn colours back into temperatures. Warmer water is a higher, brighter note, and land is silence, so you can hear the continents as gaps.
  • Air quality: the picture is split into three sections for carbon monoxide, fine particles (PM2.5) and nitrous oxides. Each pollutant has its own voice: a pluck, a soft pad and bells. Stronger colour is a higher, louder note.

Accessibility. The web page has a track chooser, large buttons, full keyboard control, labelled controls, a plain-language description of what the listener hears, and optional screen-reader announcements of where the sweep is. I tested it with NVDA. The optional Arduino device adds tactile feedback: a servo needle for the average temperature, five LEDs for the five latitude bands, and an OLED screen showing the value.

Built during the event. All the code in src/ and web/ and the final Arduino sketch were written on 14 to 15 November 2026. Before the event I only set up the repository and tools and tested the Arduino parts one at a time.

Results. Both tracks work from picture to sound to video, and the page works with a screen reader and a keyboard. The hardware demo runs in step with the sound. [Edit to match what’s true.]

Limitations.

  • Each track is built from a single frame of its video, so it is a snapshot in time, not a record of change.
  • Sea surface temperatures are approximate averages read back from the colours.
  • The air quality frame has no colour legend, so its sound shows relative strength within each pollutant. Loudness can’t be compared between pollutants, and the values are not real concentrations.
  • The air quality picture is a globe, so areas near its edge are squashed.
  • I have not yet tested it with blind or low-vision listeners.

Next steps. Use many frames so the sound follows change over time, add real concentration values for air quality, add more Earth Information Center visualizations as tracks, and work with blind and low-vision listeners to improve the sound design.
